claims.text: In a study with 46 seeded faults across three stateful services, a fresh-context independent verifier (AB) detected more seeded faults than the builder's own tests: 11 faults favored AB, 1 favored the self-verifier, and 34 were ties (Holm-corrected p=0.006).
On the two services written solely by third-party models, the independent fresh-context verifier detected 7 seeded faults that the builder's tests missed and none in the other direction (p=0.016).

A verifier from a different provider than the builder detected fewer faults than the same-model verifier: 13 faults favored the same-model verifier, none favored the other-provider verifier, and 33 were ties (Holm p=0.0005); the authors note this confounds provider and capability because only one model pair was compared.
Independent verification conditions cost 67k to 126k tokens per unit on top of the shared builder phase.
Verifier-generated tests were invalid 7 to 11% of the time, but genuine false oracles were only 0.7 to 2.3%.

The proposed framework has a specification-first phase in which the verifier sees the approved contract and public interface but not the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase using mutation analysis, property-based testing and fuzzing; the resulting assurance report leaves the release decision to a human.

For stateful requirements the specification-first verifier produces model-based tests over operation sequences, including forbidden transitions such as paying twice or refunding a payment never captured.

The authors caution that seeded faults and mutants may not represent the real faults of agent-produced code, and that hidden tests can both miss specified behavior and exceed the specification (as one EvalPlus task did).
SpecBench, which separates visible validation tests from held-out composition tests, finds that the gap between visible and held-out performance grows with code size.
MuTAP feeds surviving mutants back to an LLM to strengthen tests, and Meta's ACH generates mutants for specific fault classes and then tests that kill them.
In a study of a deployed multi-turn ordering agent, the built-in LLM judge surfaced only 2 of 9 human-confirmed systematic problem patterns in one batch (22%).
In the same ordering-agent study, the operational gate flagged zero of 100 rounds in a batch where exhaustive human review confirmed 23 distinct defects and 7 new cross-cutting patterns.
LLM-judge reliability is typically reported as agreement with human ratings rather than recall of real defects, so high agreement and low defect recall can coexist.
An audit of the hard subset of SWE-bench Verified found at least 59.4% of those problems had flawed test cases, showing eval harnesses themselves can be wrong.

LLM judges show length bias, position bias and self-preference, and are non-deterministic; the source advises using them offline on a sample, calibrated against human labels, and never as the sole release gate.
Position bias across 21 LLM judges ranged from 0.002 (Gemini 2.5 Pro) to 0.192 (Qwen 3 8B), and same-verdict rates above 95% at temperature 0 fell to as low as 70% at temperature 1.
Research cited suggests LLM-as-judge error rates can exceed 50% on complex evaluation tasks, with agreement with domain experts of 64–68% in specialized domains.
Evaluation-driven development means defining eval criteria before writing agent code and using eval results to drive architecture and prompt decisions.

Property-based testing generates hundreds or thousands of inputs to break a stated rule (tools: fast-check, Hypothesis, proptest) and shrinks failures to a minimal case, which is saved for regression testing.
Differential testing uses the old system as oracle by replaying random inputs or live traffic and checking that a replacement system's outputs match.

Trace-based auditing found frontier-backbone agents that claimed to have logged or updated state without invoking the tool and silently skipped mandatory compliance calls, failures invisible to final-answer scoring.
Vercel advises starting with the cheapest check that can catch a failure (deterministic assertions, exact match, semantic similarity) and escalating to LLM-as-judge only for judgment calls.

StrongDM's three-person AI team says humans neither write nor review generated code; agents converge against externally stored scenarios, including a Digital Twin Universe reproducing Okta, Jira, Slack, Google Drive and Google Docs.
StrongDM's digital twin approach clones external dependency behavior and runs thousands of scenarios per hour against holdout sets (company-reported, no defect-detection rates given).
Stripe reports 1,300+ agent-produced PRs merged per week, but those PRs remain human-reviewed.
